tur20-0: Most people feel better after about 2 weeks, but avoiding strenuous exercise for up to 8 weeks is advised to reduce the risk of re-injury. Once you have full strength and movement and can walk briskly without pain or swelling, start sport-specific drills and build up your training gradually. In a study of amateur athletes who tore a muscle during a sudden movement, those who started loading exercises 2 days after the injury became pain-free about 3 weeks sooner than those who started after 9 days; only one athlete had a re-injury.
tur20-1: Bayer ML, et al. Early versus delayed rehabilitation after acute muscle injury. N Engl J Med. 2017;377(13):1300–1301. Summary: MedicalResearch.com, 4 October 2017.
tur20-2: In a Swedish trial of patients with spinal stenosis causing leg pain on walking, some of whom also had a mild slip, adding screw fixation (fusion) to surgery that relieves the nerves gave no better results at 2 years, while the hospital stay and costs increased. Which operation is right is decided with your surgeon, based on the grade of the slip and how stable it is. The NORDSTEN-DS trial in Norway, which assessed 262 patients with spinal stenosis and a single-level slip of at least 3 mm, also found that surgery to relieve the nerves alone was no worse than surgery with added screw fixation: at 2 years, 71.4% versus 72.9% had at least a 30% reduction in disability score. Repeat surgery was slightly more common after decompression alone (12.5% versus 9.1%).

tur20-7: Most people recover with simple advice and by staying active. In a large UK trial of 599 people with persisting symptoms, up to six physiotherapy sessions led to slightly faster recovery at 4 months than a single advice session; there was no difference at 8 and 12 months. If your symptoms are not settling, a personalised assessment can help guide you. An Australian study of 172 people whose symptoms had lasted more than 3 months also found that a comprehensive 20-session physiotherapy exercise programme did not reduce pain more than a single advice session with telephone support at 14 weeks, 6 months or 12 months.
tur20-8: It recovers well for most people, but even with the best treatment a lag of up to 10 degrees at the end joint is common. Swelling, tenderness and redness over the back of the finger can take a few months to settle. When a piece of bone came away, a small bump may remain over the joint; this usually does not affect how the hand works. According to the British Society for Surgery of the Hand, the splint is usually worn continuously for 6–8 weeks, then for 1–2 weeks only at night and when the finger might be strained; even if the end joint stays slightly droopy, most people use their finger well. In a randomised trial of 64 people, three types of splint (a ready-made plastic splint, a padded aluminium splint and a custom heat-moulded splint) gave similar results for the remaining droop of the fingertip joint; however, treatment failed in about 24% of people with the ready-made and aluminium splints, while there were no failures with the custom splint.
tur20-9: It can. According to a Cochrane review of 10 studies with 519 people, about one in three people treated without surgery after a first dislocation had another dislocation within 2–9 years. After surgery the rate was about one in five; however, the certainty of the evidence is very low, and it is unclear whether surgery clearly improves everyday function. The rate may be higher in children and teenagers: in a study of 64 knees in under-16s whose kneecap had dislocated for the first time, followed for an average of 14 years, the kneecap dislocated again in 71% of those managed without surgery and 67% of those whose inner ligaments were repaired; surgery did not improve the long-term result, and the only factor that predicted recurrence was a family history of kneecap dislocation. A systematic review of 25 studies (920 patients) on non-surgical treatment also found a re-dislocation rate of 31%; no non-surgical method was shown to be better than another.
tur20-10: Your blood levels need to be checked first. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine’s 2024 guideline recommends measuring iron levels in everyone with restless legs syndrome and giving supplements according to the results. Taking iron you don’t need can be harmful. According to the 2018 guideline of the International Restless Legs Syndrome Study Group (IRLSSG), oral iron is possibly effective in people with a ferritin level of 75 µg/l or below; for moderate to severe symptoms, intravenous iron (ferric carboxymaltose) was found effective in people with a ferritin below 300 µg/l. Your doctor will decide which route suits you.
tur20-11: Not everyone needs an operation. Treatment usually starts with physiotherapy, cutting down on aggravating movements and painkillers; if symptoms do not settle with these, surgery may be considered. You can make the decision together with your surgeon, after talking through the possible benefits and risks. In the UK FAIT trial of 222 people in the UK, those who had keyhole hip surgery had a daily function score at 8 months that was on average 10 points better (on a 0–100 scale) than those who received up to 8 physiotherapy sessions over 5 months with activity modification.
tur20-12: No. The UK national health guideline from NICE (2025) advises against using a test or scoring tool on its own to predict falls risk; tests like this help to spot problems with walking and balance. Studies in healthy older people living independently also show that this test alone does not predict falls. So if you have fallen in the past year, tell your doctor whatever your result. If you have fallen more than once, were injured in a fall, lost consciousness or could not get up from the floor without help, you can ask for a full falls assessment. A review of 25 studies found that, using a cut-off of 13.5 seconds, the test correctly identified only about a third (31%) of people who fell; the authors recommend that it should not be used on its own.
tur20-13: Most strains improve noticeably within about 2 weeks. To avoid further damage, it is advised to avoid strenuous exercise such as running for up to 8 weeks; severe strains can take months to heal. It is safest to return to sport gradually, with a physiotherapist, once you can walk without pain and your strength has almost fully returned. In a study of 35 semi-professional football teams (652 players) in Norway, a Copenhagen adduction exercise programme done three times a week in the pre-season and once a week during the season reduced the likelihood of groin problems by 41%; continuing this kind of strengthening programme after returning to sport may be worthwhile.
tur20-14: A shoulder replacement may be considered if pain is significant and non-surgical treatment has not helped enough. Your surgeon will decide which type of replacement is suitable. A 2020 Cochrane review of 20 randomised trials (1,083 people) found no trial comparing shoulder replacement with physiotherapy or other treatments. In osteoarthritis, a total shoulder replacement may give a small benefit in pain and function over a partial replacement, but the certainty of the evidence is low.
tur20-15: Craig RS, Goodier H, Singh JA, Hopewell S, Rees JL. Shoulder replacement surgery for osteoarthritis and rotator cuff tear arthropathy. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2020;(4):CD012879.
tur20-16: In a study of 101 children, there was no difference at 3 months between waiting and watching, shock-absorbing heel cups, and physiotherapy with calf strengthening. At 6 weeks, the children using shock-absorbing heel cups were the most satisfied group; heel pain fell markedly in all three groups. So most children get better with simple measures. If the pain does not go away or keeps coming back, a personalised assessment can help guide you.
tur20-17: In a study combining data from four large ageing cohorts and published in Alzheimer's & Dementia in 2026, 54,217 people aged 50 and over without cognitive impairment at the start were followed. Regular, planned exercise and taking part in social and mental activities (community activities, hobbies, volunteering, games, learning new things) were assessed together. Compared with people low in both, the risk of cognitive impairment was 20% lower in those high only in exercise, 21% lower in those high only in social and mental engagement, and 30% lower in those high in both. From age 50, the expected time lived without cognitive impairment was estimated at 17.5 years in those low in both and 24.7 years in those high in both, a difference of about 7 years.
tur20-18: This is an observational study; it does not prove that these activities prevent cognitive impairment. The activities were self-reported, and the “high” and “low” levels are criteria harmonised across cohorts rather than guideline thresholds. The authors say the results need to be confirmed with objective measurements and intervention studies. Even so, the finding supports thinking of exercise and social and mental activity together rather than as substitutes for each other.
tur20-19: Sources: Alzheimer's & Dementia, 2026 · Medscape, 2026 · eBiotrade (in Chinese), 15 October 2026
tur20-20: In a study led by the University of Sydney and published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine in September 2026, middle-aged adults in the UK Biobank whose steps were measured with a wrist-worn device were followed for 8 years on average. Alongside daily step count, the average stepping rate (steps per minute) in the most brisk 30 minutes of the day was calculated; these minutes did not have to be consecutive. People taking fewer than 5,000 steps a day but taking them at a brisker pace had a clearly lower risk of death and of death from cardiovascular disease, similar to people taking 5,000–7,500 steps a day at a slow pace. Regardless of pace, the lowest risk was seen in those taking 7,500–10,000 steps a day; across all step groups, the lowest risk clustered around a peak pace of about 90–100 steps per minute.
tur20-21: This is an observational study; it does not prove that walking briskly extends life. Undiagnosed illnesses may have affected both step counts and risk; wrist-worn devices can also count movements other than steps, and steps were measured in only one period of the study. The authors stress that this measure should not be read as walking at that pace for 30 continuous minutes every day. The 10,000-step target came more from a 1960s Japanese pedometer campaign than from evidence; gradually increasing your current step count and walking part of it briskly is a good start.
tur20-22: Sources: British Journal of Sports Medicine, September 2026 · News-Medical, 10 September 2026 · Scripps News, 9 September 2026 · ScienceAlert, 13 September 2026
tur20-23: The PREPARE trial, run at 13 centres in Canada and published in JAMA Surgery on 3 December 2025, included 847 people aged 60 and over who were awaiting planned major surgery and scored 4 or more on a frailty scale (mean age 71.7; about three quarters were having cancer surgery). Half received a home preparation programme until surgery: one-hour strength, aerobic and flexibility exercise sessions three times a week, personalised nutrition advice and at least weekly calls with a coach; the other half were given only printed guidelines on physical activity and healthy eating. The programme lasted a median of 4 weeks. Thirty days after surgery, disability scores (WHODAS 2.0) were similar in the two groups, and in-hospital complication rates did not differ either (50.1% versus 47.7%).
tur20-24: In an exploratory additional analysis, people who completed more than 75% of the exercises had lower disability after surgery; some headlines reported, based on this analysis, that the programme reduced disability. However, such an analysis does not carry the protection of randomisation: people who stick well to a programme may already differ in other ways. Participants completed a median of 78% of the exercises; the main barriers were competing priorities and motivation. People's own rating of their health (EQ-VAS) was slightly better in the programme group. The researchers think preparation programmes may work better if there is enough time and support before surgery, and they are testing an online programme in a new trial (STRIVE).
tur20-25: Sources: JAMA Surgery, 2026;161(2):113–123 · Ottawa Hospital Research Institute, 3 December 2025 · HealthDay, 11 December 2025
tur20-26: No. In a large observational study published in 2026, the lowest risk was seen in people taking 7,500–10,000 steps a day; but even among people taking fewer than 5,000 steps a day, taking some of them at a brisk pace was linked to lower risk. The 10,000-step target came more from a 1960s Japanese pedometer campaign than from evidence. Gradually increasing your current step count and walking part of it briskly is a good start.
